title:
At Wenming Garden Dong Zhuo roars at Ding Yuan
With gold and pearls Li Su wins over Lü Bu
paragraphs:
[Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) said to [He Jin](char-he-jin) that day: "The mischief of eunuchs is no new thing. But rulers should never have lent them power and favor, and let it come to this. If they are to be punished, cut off the chief offender — one jailer is enough for the work. What need of all this calling up of troops from outside? Try to kill them to the last man and the design is sure to get out. I say it must fail." "Does Mengde too harbor some purpose of his own?" said He Jin angrily. As he withdrew Cao Cao said: "The man who throws the realm into disorder will be He Jin." So He Jin sent his messengers out in secret with the sealed edicts, riding through the night to the garrisons.
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) was at this time General of the Vanguard, Marquis of Aoxiang and Inspector of Xiliang. He had won nothing against the Yellow Turbans, and the court would have called him to account for it, but a bribe to the Ten Attendants saved him; afterwards he attached himself to the great men of the court, rose to high office, and held two hundred thousand of the armies of the west, with a disloyal heart in him all the while. The edict came, to his delight. He mustered his men and sent them off division by division, left his son-in-law [Niu Fu](char-niu-fu), a General of the Household, to hold Shaanxi, and marched on [Luoyang](loc-luoyang) himself with [Li Jue](char-li-jue), [Guo Si](char-guo-si), [Zhang Ji](char-zhang-ji) and [Fan Chou](char-fan-chou). Dong Zhuo's son-in-law and counselor [Li Ru](char-li-ru) said: "We have the edict, but there is much in it that is not above board. Send up a memorial. Then we come openly and with good warrant, and the great design may be carried through." Dong Zhuo was well pleased, and sent one up. The substance of it ran: "Your servant has heard that rebellion in the realm never ceases, and that the whole of it comes of [Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) and the Yellow Gate Attendants, who flout the constant law of Heaven. It is said that to stop a pot boiling it is better to take away the firewood than to ladle the water, and that to lance an abscess, though it hurt, is better than to nurse the poison. Your servant makes bold to enter Luoyang with bell and drum and rid the court of Zhang Rang and his fellows, to the great good of the altars and the great good of the realm!"
[He Jin](char-he-jin) received the memorial and showed it to the ministers. Zheng Tai, an Imperial Clerk, spoke against it: "[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) is a wolf. Bring him into the capital and he will eat men." "You see danger everywhere," said He Jin. "You are no man to plan a great business with." [Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi) urged the same. "I know Dong Zhuo of old — a kindly face and a savage heart. Let him once inside the palace and there will be mischief for certain. Better stop him from coming at all, and spare ourselves the disorder."
[He Jin](char-he-jin) would not listen, and Zheng Tai and [Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi) both gave up their offices and went, with more than half the great men of the court after them. He Jin sent to meet [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) at Mianchi, and there Dong Zhuo halted his troops and did not stir. [Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) and the rest heard that the provincial troops had come. "This is He Jin's doing," they said among themselves. "Strike first, or our clans will be wiped out." So they laid fifty men with swords and axes in hiding inside the Jiade Gate of the Changle Palace, and went in to [Empress Dowager He](char-empress-he). "The Grand General has forged an edict and called provincial troops up to the capital to destroy us. We look to Your Majesty's pity to save us." "Go to the Grand General's residence and ask his pardon," said the Empress Dowager. "If we go to his house," said Zhang Rang, "we shall be ground to dust, flesh and bone together. We beg Your Majesty to summon the Grand General into the palace and bid him let the matter drop. If he will not hear you, let us die here in your presence."
So the [Empress Dowager](char-empress-he) sent out her summons, and [He Jin](char-he-jin) set off the moment it came. [Chen Lin](char-chen-lin) the Registrar spoke against it: "This summons of the Empress Dowager's is the Ten Attendants' work for certain. You must not go. Nothing but harm can come of it." "The Empress Dowager summons me. What harm should there be?" said He Jin. [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) said: "Now that the plot is out and the matter known, General, would you still walk into the palace?" "Call the Ten Attendants out first, and then you may go in," said [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao). He Jin laughed. "A child's view. I hold the power of the realm in my hand. What dare the Ten Attendants do?" "If you are set on going, we will bring armed men as escort, against anything unlooked for," said Yuan Shao.
So [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) and [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) each picked five hundred of their best men and gave the command of them to Yuan Shao's brother [Yuan Shu](char-yuan-shu). Yuan Shu put on his full harness and drew the men up outside the Qingsuo Gate, while Yuan Shao and Cao Cao, swords at their sides, brought [He Jin](char-he-jin) as far as the front of the Changle Palace. There a [Yellow Gate](misc-yellow-gate) eunuch came out with the Empress Dowager's word: "Her Majesty summons the Grand General alone. No one else may come in." Yuan Shao and Cao Cao and the rest were held at the palace gate, and He Jin walked in with his head high. At the door of the Jiade Hall [Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) and [Duan Gui](char-duan-gui) came out to meet him, their men closed round him on both sides, and a great fear took He Jin. Zhang Rang rated him in a hard voice: "What was [Empress Dong](char-empress-dowager-dong)'s crime, that she should be poisoned out of the way? When the mother of the realm was buried, you pleaded sickness and would not come! You are a butcher's brat, and it was we who commended you to the Son of Heaven and made your fortune; yet instead of repaying it you plot our deaths! You call us foul; who then is clean?" He Jin lost his head and looked for a way out, but every gate was shut, and the men in hiding came out together and hacked him in two. A later poet sighed over him:
> The house of Han was sinking to its fate,
> And witless He Jin sat among the great.
> Oft warned by loyal men, he scorned them all,
> And took the sword's edge in the palace hall.
When [Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) and the rest had killed [He Jin](char-he-jin), [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) waited a long while outside and saw nothing of him, and called out at the palace gate: "Your carriage is waiting, General!" For answer they threw He Jin's head over the wall and proclaimed: "He Jin plotted treason and has been put to death. The rest of you were forced into his following and are pardoned." Yuan Shao raised a great shout: "The eunuchs have murdered a great minister! Let whoever would kill the wicked crew come out and fight!" Then Wu Kuang, one of He Jin's officers, set fire to the Qingsuo Gate from outside, and [Yuan Shu](char-yuan-shu) broke into the palace courts with his men and killed every eunuch he found, high or low. Yuan Shao and [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) hacked through the bars and went in after them. [Zhao Zhong](char-zhao-zhong), [Cheng Kuang](char-cheng-kuang), [Xia Yun](char-xia-yun) and [Guo Sheng](char-guo-sheng) were run down in front of the Cuihua Tower and chopped to a pulp. The flames in the palace went up to heaven. Zhang Rang, [Duan Gui](char-duan-gui), [Cao Jie](char-cao-jie) and [Hou Lan](char-hou-lan) carried off the [Empress Dowager](char-empress-he), the [young Emperor](char-prince-bian) and the [Prince of Chenliu](char-prince-xie) to the inner apartments, and fled by the back way to the North Palace.
[Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi) had given up his office but had not yet left the capital. Seeing the palace in uproar, he put on his mail, took a dagger-axe and stood below the gallery. From a distance he saw [Duan Gui](char-duan-gui) hustling the [Empress Dowager](char-empress-he) along, and roared out: "Traitor Duan Gui! How dare you carry off the Empress Dowager!" Duan Gui turned and ran. The Empress Dowager jumped from a window, and Lu Zhi got to her in time and brought her off safe. Wu Kuang fought his way into the inner court and found [He Miao](char-he-miao) coming out with a drawn sword. "He Miao had a hand in his own brother's murder," he shouted. "Let us kill him together!" "Cut the traitor down!" the men answered with one voice. He Miao turned to run, but they ringed him round and cut him to pieces. [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) then sent soldiers out in parties to kill the households of the Ten Attendants, old and young alike, and not one was left alive; many a beardless man was killed in error. [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) meanwhile put out the fires in the palace, begged the Empress Dowager to take the government in hand for the time, sent troops after [Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang), and set men to look for the [young Emperor](char-prince-bian).
[Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) and [Duan Gui](char-duan-gui), meanwhile, had carried the [young Emperor](char-prince-bian) and the [Prince of Chenliu](char-prince-xie) off through the smoke and fire, and ran with them all night as far as [Mount Beimang](loc-beimang). About the third watch a great shouting rose behind them and horse and foot came up, with Min Gong, an officer of the central division of Henan, at their head, crying: "Halt, traitors!" Zhang Rang saw there was no escape, and threw himself into the river and drowned. The Emperor and the Prince of Chenliu did not know what was behind the noise, and dared not call out, but lay hidden in the rough grass of the bank. The horsemen scattered to search, but did not find where the Emperor was.
The [Emperor](char-prince-bian) and the [Prince of Chenliu](char-prince-xie) lay there till the fourth watch. The dew came down, they were faint with hunger, and they clung to one another and wept, swallowing their sobs in the grass for fear of being heard. "We cannot stay here long," said the Prince of Chenliu. "We must find some other way out." So the two knotted their clothes together and climbed the bank. Thorns grew thick on every side, and in the dark no road showed. They were at their wits' end when of a sudden a swarm of fireflies came up in their hundreds, and their light went circling before the Emperor. "Heaven is helping us two brothers!" said the Prince of Chenliu. They followed the fireflies, and little by little a path appeared. By the fifth watch their feet were too sore to carry them further. Beside the hill was a heap of straw, and the two lay down at the foot of it. In front of the heap stood a farm. That night its master had dreamed of two red suns falling behind his house; he woke in alarm, threw on his clothes and went out to look about him, and saw a red light shooting up to the sky above the straw heap behind the farm. He hurried over, and there they were, lying beside the straw.
"Whose sons are you two boys?" asked the master of the farm. The [Emperor](char-prince-bian) dared not answer. The [Prince of Chenliu](char-prince-xie) pointed to him. "This is the Emperor who reigns today. He fled here out of the disorder the Ten Attendants have made. I am his brother, the Prince of Chenliu." The man was astonished, and bowed twice. "I am Cui Yi, brother of Cui Lie, who was Minister of the Masses in the last reign. I have lived hidden here since I saw the Ten Attendants selling offices and hounding good men." He helped the Emperor into the house and knelt to set food and wine before him.
Min Gong, meanwhile, had overtaken [Duan Gui](char-duan-gui) and seized him, and asked where the Son of Heaven was. Duan Gui said they had parted on the road and he did not know where he had gone. So Min Gong killed him, hung the head at his horse's neck, divided his men to search in every direction, and rode on alone along the road. He came by chance to Cui Yi's farm. Cui Yi saw the head and asked about it, and Min Gong told him the whole of it; so Cui Yi brought him in to the [Emperor](char-prince-bian), and sovereign and servant wept together. "The country cannot be a single day without its lord," said Min Gong. "I beg Your Majesty to return to the capital." There was only one lean horse on the farm, and they saddled it for the Emperor; Min Gong and the [Prince of Chenliu](char-prince-xie) rode another between them. They had not gone three li from the farm when [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun), Minister of the Masses, [Yang Biao](char-yang-biao), Grand Commandant, [Chunyu Qiong](char-chunyu-qiong), Colonel of the Left Army, Zhao Meng, Colonel of the Right Army, [Bao Xin](char-bao-xin), Colonel of the Rear Army, and [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao), Colonel of the Central Army, came up with several hundred men and horse and met the imperial party; there was weeping on all sides. Duan Gui's head was sent ahead to be shown in the capital, good horses were brought for the Emperor and the Prince of Chenliu, and they rode back to the city with a press of men about them. There had been a rhyme among the children of [Luoyang](loc-luoyang) before this:
> Emperor is emperor none,
> Prince is prince no more;
> Car on car, horse on horse, to [Beimang](loc-beimang) pour.
Thus was the prophecy fulfilled.
They had not gone many li more when banners darkened the sun and dust hid the sky, and a body of troops came up. The officials turned pale, and the [Emperor](char-prince-bian) was badly frightened. [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) spurred out and asked who they were. Out from the shadow of the embroidered flags flew a general, who called in a hard voice: "Where is the Son of Heaven?" The Emperor shook and could not speak. The [Prince of Chenliu](char-prince-xie) reined his horse forward. "Who comes there?" he said sharply. "[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), Inspector of Xiliang." "Have you come to guard the imperial carriage, or to seize it?" "I have come to guard it." "Then since you come to guard it, and the Son of Heaven is here, why are you not off your horse?" Dong Zhuo was taken aback. He scrambled down in haste and made his bow at the left of the road. The Prince of Chenliu spoke to him and put him at his ease, and from first to last there was not a word out of place. Dong Zhuo wondered at him privately, and from that hour he had it in mind to set another on the throne.
That day they came back to the palace and saw [Empress Dowager He](char-empress-he), and all of them wept bitterly. When the palace was gone through, the [Heirloom Seal of the Realm](misc-heirloom-seal) was missing. [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) camped his army outside the walls and came into the city every day with his mailed horse, riding through the streets as he pleased, and the people lived in dread. He went in and out of the palace itself with hardly a show of deference. [Bao Xin](char-bao-xin), Colonel of the Rear Army, came to [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) and told him that Dong Zhuo certainly meant mischief and should be put down at once. "The court is only just settled," said Yuan Shao. "We must not move lightly." Bao Xin went to [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun) and said the same. "Let it wait till we have talked it over," said Wang Yun. So Bao Xin took his own troops and went off to Mount Tai.
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) drew over the troops that had served [He Jin](char-he-jin) and his brother, until the whole of them were in his hand. "I have a mind to put down the [Emperor](char-prince-bian) and set up the [Prince of Chenliu](char-prince-xie)," he said privately to [Li Ru](char-li-ru). "What do you say?" "The court is without a master," said Li Ru. "If it is not done now, delay will bring a change. Tomorrow call the officials together in the Wenming Garden and tell them the Emperor is to be changed. Cut down whoever will not have it. Today is the day to make your authority good."
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) was pleased. Next day he laid out a great feast and invited the whole of the nobility, and not one of them dared stay away, for they all feared him. He waited until the officials were assembled, then came slowly down to the garden gate, dismounted, and walked to his place with his sword on. When the wine had gone round several times he had it stopped and the music silenced, and said in a hard voice: "I have something to say. Let the officers hear it in silence." Every man turned his ear. "The Son of Heaven is lord of all the people," said Dong Zhuo, "and without presence and dignity he cannot serve the ancestral temple and the altars of the land. The [Emperor](char-prince-bian) who now reigns is a weakling. He is not the equal of the [Prince of Chenliu](char-prince-xie), who is quick and fond of his books and fit to take the great seat. I mean to put down the Emperor and set up the Prince of Chenliu. What do the ministers say?" Not one dared make a sound. Then a man pushed back the table and standing before the feast he cried: "It shall not be! Who are you, that you dare talk so high? The Son of Heaven is the late Emperor's lawful son and has done no wrong. What right have you to talk of putting down an emperor? Would you be a usurper?" Dong Zhuo looked: it was [Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan), Inspector of Jing Province. "Who follows me lives; who crosses me dies!" Dong Zhuo roared at him, and drew his sword to cut Ding Yuan down.
Just then [Li Ru](char-li-ru) saw the man standing behind [Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan) — of a lofty bearing and a commanding presence, holding a crescent-bladed halberd, his eyes blazing. Li Ru stepped up quickly. "This is a drinking party, and no place to talk of state affairs. Tomorrow at the council hall will be soon enough to debate it in the open." The company all urged Ding Yuan to his horse, and he rode away. [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) turned to the officials. "Have I not spoken justly?" [Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi) answered: "Your Excellency is wrong. In the old days Tai Jia was unfit to rule, and [Yi Yin](char-yi-yin) banished him to the Tong palace; the Prince of Changyi had been twenty-seven days on the throne and had done above three thousand wicked things, so [Huo Guang](char-huo-guang) announced it in the ancestral temple and put him down. The [Emperor](char-prince-bian) who now reigns is young, but he is quick and humane and wise, and has not a hair's weight of fault in him. You are an Inspector of an outer commandery, have had no share in the government, and have none of the great gifts of Yi Yin or Huo Guang. By what right would you force through a change of emperors? The sage says: 'With Yi Yin's purpose it may be done; without Yi Yin's purpose it is usurpation.'" Dong Zhuo in a great rage drew his sword and came at him to kill him. Peng Bo, a Court Counselor, spoke up: "Lu Zhi of the Secretariat is looked up to throughout the land. Cut him down first, and I fear the whole realm will take fright." At that Dong Zhuo held his hand. [Wang Yun](char-wang-yun), Minister of the Masses, said: "A matter of deposing and enthroning is not to be settled over wine. Let us debate it another day." So the officials all dispersed. Dong Zhuo stood at the garden gate with his hand on his sword, and saw a man wheeling his horse up and down outside, a halberd in his hand. He asked Li Ru who it was. "That is Ding Yuan's foster son," said Li Ru. "Lü is his surname, [Bu](char-lu-bu) his name, Fengxian his style. You had better keep out of his way, my lord." So Dong Zhuo went into the garden out of sight.
Next day word came that [Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan) had brought his army outside the walls and offered battle. [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) in anger led his own men out with [Li Ru](char-li-ru) to meet him. The two lines drew up facing, and there was [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) with a gold coronet binding his hair, a battle robe figured with a hundred flowers, a coat of beast-hide mail and a jewelled belt with lions worked upon it; he put his horse forward with his halberd levelled and rode out before the line at Ding Yuan's side. Ding Yuan pointed at Dong Zhuo and cursed him: "The country is in misfortune, the eunuchs have played with power, and the people are in the mire for it. You have not an inch of merit to your name. How dare you talk idly of putting down an emperor and throwing the court into confusion?"
Before [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) could answer, [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) flew at him on his horse. Dong Zhuo turned and ran, [Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan) brought his army on after him, and Dong Zhuo's men were badly beaten. He fell back more than thirty li, made his camp and called his people together. "Lü Bu is no ordinary man," he said. "If I had him, what trouble could the realm give me?" A man came out from the front of the tent. "My lord, set your mind at rest. Lü Bu and I are from the same village, and I know him for a brave man without judgment, who forgets his honor at the sight of a profit. My tongue shall bring him in with folded hands. What do you say to it?"
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) was delighted. He looked, and it was [Li Su](char-li-su), an officer of the Tiger Guards. "How will you work on him?" "I hear you have a famous horse, my lord, called [Red Hare](misc-red-hare), that goes a thousand li in a day," said Li Su. "Let me have the horse, and gold and pearls besides, to bind his heart with profit. Then I will put my arguments to him, and [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) will turn against [Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan) and come over to you for certain." Dong Zhuo asked [Li Ru](char-li-ru) whether the plan would serve. "You would have the realm, my lord," said Li Ru. "What is one horse to grudge?" Dong Zhuo gave the horse gladly, and a thousand liang of gold with it, several dozen bright pearls, and a jade belt.
[Li Su](char-li-su) took the presents and rode to [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu)'s camp, where the pickets closed round him. "Tell General Lü quickly that an old friend has come to see him," he said. The soldiers took in word, and Lü Bu had him brought in. "Brother, no ills since we parted, I hope!" said Li Su. Lü Bu bowed. "It is long since we met. Where are you living now?" "I hold the post of General of the Tiger Guards. I was glad past telling to hear that you are upholding the altars of the land. I have a good horse that goes a thousand li in a day and crosses water and climbs hills as on level ground; he is called [Red Hare](misc-red-hare), and I have brought him as a gift to you, brother, to aid a tiger's strength." Lü Bu had the horse led up to look at. Red he was from head to foot, the red of burning coal, without a hair of another color on him, a zhang long from head to tail and eight chi high from hoof to neck; and when he neighed and roared he seemed ready to mount the sky or plunge into the sea. A later poet wrote of the Red Hare:
> A thousand li at speed, and dust-clouds fly;
> Through flood and hill the purple mists roll by.
> The silken rein is snapped, the jade bit shakes;
> A fire-dragon from the ninth heaven breaks.
[Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) was overjoyed with the horse and thanked [Li Su](char-li-su). "Brother, you give me such a steed. How am I to repay it?" "I came for honor's sake," said Li Su. "What repayment should I seek?" Lü Bu set wine before him. When the wine was in them Li Su said: "You and I see little of each other, brother, but I meet your father often enough." "You are drunk!" said Lü Bu. "My father has been many years out of the world. How should you be meeting him?" Li Su laughed aloud. "Not he. I mean your father of today, Inspector Ding." Lü Bu looked abashed. "I am with Ding Jianyang because I have no choice." "You have it in you to hold up the sky and bridle the sea, brother," said Li Su. "Who within the four seas does not look up to you? Rank and fame and riches are in your reach, as easy as putting your hand in a bag. Why talk of having no choice, and stand under another man?" "I have not found my master, that is all," said Lü Bu. Li Su smiled. "A good bird chooses its tree to roost in, and a wise servant chooses his lord to serve. Be slow to see your chance, and repentance will come too late." "You are at court," said Lü Bu. "Who do you see there that is the hero of the age?" Li Su answered: "I have looked them all over, and there is not one the equal of [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo). He honors the worthy and is courteous to men of talent, his rewards and punishments are clear, and he will come to great things in the end." "I would follow him," said Lü Bu, "but I have no way to reach him."
[Li Su](char-li-su) brought out the gold and the pearls and the jade belt and laid them before him. [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) was startled. "What is all this for?" Li Su had the attendants sent out of the room. "[Lord Dong](char-dong-zhuo) has long admired your great name, and sent me with these. The [Red Hare](misc-red-hare) is his gift too." "If Lord Dong holds me so dear, how am I to repay him?" said Lü Bu. "A man of small ability like myself is a General of the Tiger Guards," said Li Su. "If you go to him there is no saying how high you will stand." "Yet I have not a grain of merit to bring him as a present on first meeting." "The merit is there for the turning of a hand, if only you are willing." Lü Bu sat a long while over it. "I have a mind to kill [Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan) and bring my men over to [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo). What do you say?" Li Su said: "If you will, brother, there can be no greater service! But the business will not bear delay. Settle it quickly."
[Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) promised [Li Su](char-li-su) to come over the next day, and Li Su took his leave. That night about the second watch Lü Bu walked into [Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan)'s tent with a sword in his hand. Ding Yuan was reading by candlelight, and looked up as he came in. "What brings my son here?" "I am a man in my own right," said Lü Bu. "Why should I be your son?" "Fengxian, what has changed your heart?" Lü Bu went forward and took Ding Yuan's head off at a stroke, then shouted to those about him: "I have killed Ding Yuan for his cruelty! Let those who will follow me stay. Those who will not may go!" More than half the soldiers dispersed.
Next day [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) carried [Ding Yuan](char-ding-yuan)'s head to [Li Su](char-li-su), who took him in to [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo). Dong Zhuo was overjoyed and set wine before him, and bowed to him first. "General, to have you today is like a parched field getting sweet rain." Lü Bu seated him and made his own bow. "If you will not refuse me, let me do you reverence as my foster father." Dong Zhuo gave him golden armor and a brocade robe, and they drank deep and parted. From that day Dong Zhuo's power and prestige grew greater still. He took the office of General of the Vanguard upon himself, made his brother [Dong Min](char-dong-min) General of the Left and Marquis of Hu, and made Lü Bu Cavalry Commandant, General of the Household and Marquis of the Capital Village. [Li Ru](char-li-ru) pressed him to settle the matter of the deposition quickly, so Dong Zhuo set out a feast in the palace, gathered the nobility, and had Lü Bu stand guard on either hand with a thousand men in mail.
That day [Yuan Wei](char-yuan-wei), the Grand Tutor, came with the whole body of officials. When the wine had gone round a few times [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) drew his sword. "The [Emperor](char-prince-bian) who now reigns is dull and weak, unfit to serve the ancestral temple. I shall do as [Yi Yin](char-yi-yin) and [Huo Guang](char-huo-guang) did before me: put him down to be Prince of Hongnong and set up the [Prince of Chenliu](char-prince-xie) as Emperor. Whoever will not have it dies!" The ministers were terrified, and not one dared answer. Then [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao), Colonel of the Central Army, stepped straight out. "The Emperor has not been long on the throne and has done nothing to forfeit it. You would put down the son of the Empress and set up the son of a lesser consort. What is that but treason?" Dong Zhuo said in a rage: "The business of the realm lies with me! Who dares refuse? Do you think my sword not sharp?" Yuan Shao drew his own. "Your sword is sharp. But mine no less!" And the two faced each other. Truly:
> Ding Yuan stood for the right, and first lay dead;
> Yuan Shao now bares his blade, and risks his head.
Whether Yuan Shao kept his life, the next chapter will tell.
